opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it changes almost everything about the interface, even though the underlying problem, finding the right information on the web, stays the same.

The search engines we grew up with were designed around a human's constraints. A person types two or three words, looks at ten blue links, scans snippets, clicks one or two, and decides for themselves what's trustworthy. The whole system is optimized for scarce human attention: rank a handful of results well, keep the page fast and clean, and let the person do the reasoning.

An agent has completely different constraints. It doesn't type a short keyword query. It can express a rich, detailed intent: "find me every company that changed its pricing in the last quarter, with the source and the date." It doesn't want ten links to click through. It wants the actual content, the relevant passages, structured in a way it can reason over and drop straight into its context window. And it doesn't get tired. It's happy to issue hundreds of queries, go deep, and spend more compute when the task warrants it.

So I think the interface moves from "query in, ranked links out" to something more like "objective in, evidence out." You describe what you're trying to accomplish, maybe how much latency or cost you're willing to trade for quality, and the system gives you dense, relevant information with provenance attached: where it came from, how fresh it is, how confident we are. Provenance matters a lot here, because the agent and ultimately the human downstream need to verify claims, not just consume them.

The other shift is in what you optimize for. With humans, you're optimizing for clicks and satisfaction on a results page. With agents, you're optimizing for whether the agent completes its task correctly. That's a much more measurable target in some ways, and it lets you build the whole stack, indexing, retrieval, ranking, extraction, around being useful to a machine reader rather than a human skimmer.

Longer term, I expect agents to be the dominant users of the web, by volume, by a wide margin. If that's true, we need infrastructure built for them from first principles, and that includes thinking about how the open web stays healthy, how publishers get value, and how trust works when most of the reading is done by software. Retrofitting human search for agents won't be enough. It needs to be rebuilt.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can provide rich, detailed intent and that this enables the search system to return dense, relevant information tailored to the task.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that almost everything we think of as "search" was designed around a human constraint, and that constraint goes away when the user is a model.

Think about what a search results page actually is. It's ten blue links, a snippet, maybe a knowledge panel. That format exists because a human can only read so much, so fast. We optimized for a person scanning, clicking, coming back, refining their query. Every design decision, from ranking to snippets to the ten-result cap, is really a bet about human attention.

An agent doesn't have that constraint. It can consume a hundred documents in the time it takes a person to read one snippet. So the first thing that changes is that the output stops being a ranked list optimized for a click and becomes something much closer to raw, high-density evidence. The agent doesn't want you to pick the best result for it. It wants the full set of relevant material, with provenance, so it can do its own reasoning over it.

The second thing that changes is the query itself. Humans type two or three keywords because that's what works, and the engine has spent twenty years learning to infer intent from almost nothing. An agent can tell you exactly what it's trying to do. It can say, "I'm trying to verify this claim, here's the context, here's what I already know, here's what would change my mind." That's a fundamentally richer signal, and a search system built for agents should accept that whole context, not just a string.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that search becomes a multi-step conversation rather than a single transaction. A human does one query, maybe a couple. An agent working on a real task might do fifty, each one shaped by what it learned from the last. So latency matters differently, freshness matters differently, and the system needs to understand it's in a loop with the agent rather than serving a one-off request.

The way I'd frame it is that search for humans is a product. Search for agents is infrastructure. It's the retrieval layer the whole reasoning stack sits on top of, and if that layer is slow, stale, or shaped for a human eyeball, every agent built on it inherits those limitations. Getting that layer right is, I think, one of the more important and less glamorous problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can provide its full task context and that search systems should accept it, describing this richer signal as enabling better agent-oriented search.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that search becomes less about presenting a page of results and more about providing information an agent can use to complete a task. For a human, you’re optimizing for something they can scan, understand, and click through. An agent may need structured information, the underlying sources, and enough context to decide whether it has an answer or needs to keep looking.

And the interaction can be much more iterative. The agent can ask a question, examine what comes back, and ask a more specific question. So the interface needs to support that loop efficiently. It’s less about getting one perfect query and more about helping the agent make progress, while preserving the evidence behind its answer.

r001.rationale: The response says agents need structured information, sources, context, and an iterative search loop. It does not state that giving the search engine more information from the agent helps it serve the agent better.

sol-6.1.text:
When a human uses search, you give them a page of results, and they do a lot of the work: opening links, reading, comparing sources, deciding what to trust. An agent can take on more of that work, so the interface doesn’t need to look like a search results page.

It needs to provide information the agent can use—relevant passages, where they came from, and enough context to interpret them correctly. And it becomes more iterative. The agent searches, learns something, realizes what’s missing, and searches again.

So I think the shift is from an interface designed around human attention to one designed around completing a task. The question becomes: can you get the agent the right evidence, reliably and quickly enough, to take the next step?

r001.rationale: The response says the agent searches again as it learns what is missing, but does not state that giving the search engine more information from the agent helps it serve the agent better.
